slides.text: Pt. Madhavrao Sapre was the first to inspire the development and national awakening of Chhattisgarh. In 1900, he published the first monthly magazine of Chhattisgarh — Chhattisgarh Mitra — from Pendrawan and inspired the people.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: Madhavrao Sapre at a printing press in lamplight, 1900, the first issue of Chhattisgarh Mitra being printed. Fresh ink on paper. A pen as sword. Title: Awakening. Warm sepia tones, the birth of a new era of resistance.

slides.text: In 1889, during the Bombay session of the Indian National Congress, the leaders of the Central Province came together. Among the 214 delegates who attended were CM Thakkar, Pt. Ramdayal Tiwari, Madhavrao Sapre, and Vamanrao Lakhe — the first sons of Chhattisgarh at the national table.
slides.visualDescription: The Bombay Congress session of 1889 — a grand hall, 214 delegates. Among them, four faces from Chhattisgarh highlighted: CM Thakkar, Pt. Ramdayal Tiwari, Madhavrao Sapre, Vamanrao Lakhe. Chhattisgarh enters the national conversation.

slides.text: After attending the Congress party conventions, leaders like Madhavrao Sapre and Vamanrao Lakhe returned and started anti-British awakening in their respective areas. The seeds of organised resistance were planted across the region.
slides.visualDescription: Sapre and Lakhe returning from Bombay by train — looking out the window at their homeland with new eyes. On arrival, gathering villagers, speaking under a Banyan tree. Seeds of consciousness being planted in the soil of Chhattisgarh.

slides.text: In 1900, Pt. Madhavrao Sapre published Chhattisgarh Mitra — the first monthly magazine of the region — from Pendrawan. It was the first voice of organised political consciousness in Chhattisgarh. The word, after the sword, becomes the weapon.
slides.visualDescription: The printing press at Pendrawan, 1900. The first issue of Chhattisgarh Mitra coming off the press. Sapre reading the fresh copy, holding it up to lamplight. The first written voice of Chhattisgarh's resistance. Ink and determination.

slides.text: The Arya Samaj established in Raipur brought social reform — against untouchability, for widow marriage, for women's education. A religious organisation becoming an agent of social revolution. Reform and resistance traveling together.
slides.visualDescription: An Arya Samaj gathering in Raipur — men and women of all castes seated together. A widow allowed to sit in the front row. A Harijan child receiving education alongside upper-caste children. Social revolution wearing religious clothes.

slides.text: In 1905, the Swadeshi Movement reached Chhattisgarh following the Partition of Bengal. The boycott of British goods — cloth, sugar, salt — became the first mass economic weapon against the empire. The charkha was not yet symbol; it was survival.
slides.visualDescription: A bonfire of British cloth in a Raipur market, 1905. Merchants and farmers watching, some apprehensive, some exhilarated. Imported cloth burning. Local khadi being displayed beside it. The Swadeshi Movement as economic warfare. Visual energy.

slides.text: The Goraksha Song — written by Wali Mohammad — united Hindu and Muslim communities under one anthem: 'Gaiyya roi, roi karat pukaar, More praan bacha lo hari.' A Muslim man writing a Hindu devotional song as an act of nationalist solidarity.
slides.visualDescription: Wali Mohammad — a Muslim writer — at his desk composing the Goraksha Song. Hindu and Muslim villagers singing it together in the street. The words: Gaiyya roi, roi karat pukaar — a cow weeping, calling for help. Unity through shared devotion.

slides.text: In 1906, CM Thakkar founded the Congress in Raipur. Pt. Sundarlal Sharma joined the Congress around this time, bringing with him his work on untouchability and his deep roots in the villages of Chhattisgarh.
slides.visualDescription: The founding meeting of the Congress in Raipur, 1906. CM Thakkar presiding. Pt. Sundarlal Sharma — a man of visible integrity — sitting in the front. The Congress flag being raised for the first time in Chhattisgarh. History with a small beginning.

slides.text: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma — a zamindar who gave up privilege for reform — was already fighting untouchability before Gandhi made it his central cause. He was conducting Janeu movements, making people of all castes equal before the sacred thread.
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma placing the sacred thread on a Harijan man — the Janeu ceremony performed for those traditionally denied it. Upper-caste observers watching, some shocked, some moved. A zamindar dismantling caste hierarchy with a thread.

slides.text: In the year 1914, the campaign to close slaughterhouses in villages Karmandih and Ghobani succeeded entirely through non-violent people's pressure — no violence, no litigation. An early proof that Satyagraha could work before Gandhi named it here.
slides.visualDescription: Villagers of Karmandih gathering peacefully outside a slaughterhouse — sitting, praying, blocking the entrance through sheer moral presence. The slaughterhouse owner closing the doors. A small victory. A method proved. Non-violence before Gandhi arrived.

slides.text: In 1907, the Surat split divided the Congress into Garam Dal and Naram Dal. Chhattisgarh produced leaders on both sides — its movement broad enough to contain both the aggressive and the moderate visions of independence.
slides.visualDescription: The Surat Congress session of 1907 — the dramatic split between Tilak's Garam Dal and Gokhale's Naram Dal. Chhattisgarh leaders on both sides of the hall. The region as a mirror of the national debate. Unity of purpose, diversity of method.

slides.text: The Home Rule League arrived in Chhattisgarh in 1917. Ravi Shankar Shukla, E. Raghavendra Rao, Thakur Pyarelal Singh, and Ghanshyam Singh Gupta — each building branches, each weaving the region into the national fabric of resistance.
slides.visualDescription: 1917. Home Rule League meetings spreading across Chhattisgarh — Raipur, Dhamtari, Bilaspur, Durg. Four leaders at four tables in four cities. Maps being drawn, members being enrolled. Chhattisgarh networking itself into the national movement.

slides.text: The 1918 Sixth Provincial Conference held in Raipur was a landmark. Shukla chairs. Raghavendra Rao organises. The Tilak era is at its height. Chhattisgarh is no longer a peripheral province — it is an active voice in the freedom movement.
slides.visualDescription: The Sixth Provincial Conference, Raipur, 1918. A formal gathering of leaders from across the Central Province. Ravi Shankar Shukla chairing the session. Chhattisgarh at the center of the provincial movement. Confidence, organisation, purpose.

slides.text: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma's 21-day fast against untouchability became a defining act. Chhabilal Choubey fasted alongside him. The fast as a weapon — not the hunger strike of weakness, but the supreme moral assertion of strength.
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma in a sparse room — 21 days of fasting. Thin, but resolute. Chhabilal Choubey beside him, equally determined. Crowds gathering outside, moved by the moral force of the act. Sacrifice as argument. Hunger as truth.

slides.text: Dau Tularam Parganiha became the first graduate of Chhattisgarh. Daulatram Mishra became the first barrister. The pen and the courtroom — new arenas of resistance. The third generation of Chhattisgarh's freedom movement is educated and organised.
slides.visualDescription: Dau Tularam Parganiha holding his graduation scroll. Daulatram Mishra in barrister's robes. Two firsts for Chhattisgarh. Education as empowerment. The British legal system being learned in order to be turned against the British. New weapons.

slides.text: Ravi Shankar Shukla was first arrested in 1919 for leading the Home Rule agitation in Raipur. He was released and immediately returned to organising. Each arrest only deepened his commitment and expanded his following.
slides.visualDescription: Ravi Shankar Shukla being led away by British officers after his first arrest, 1919. The crowd watching. His expression: calm, unbroken. Then his release — the crowd welcoming him back. The cycle of arrest and return as the rhythm of leadership.

slides.text: The Khilafat Movement brought Hindu-Muslim unity to Chhattisgarh's freedom struggle. Muslim zamindars sacrificed their land and Malguzari for the movement. Mohammad Yunus, among others, chose jail over compliance.
slides.visualDescription: A Muslim zamindar signing away his land for the Khilafat movement. The documents of sacrifice. Hindu and Muslim leaders sitting together at a Congress session. Mohammad Yunus standing before a British magistrate — unflinching. Unity made visible.

slides.text: Asgar Ali thanked the Hindu brethren for their sympathy for the Muslim cause. Ravi Shankar Shukla retorted: 'We are no more Hindu and Muslims, but Hindustanis in the strictest sense.' These words echoed across the district like a bell.
slides.visualDescription: The Khilafat sub-committee meeting in Raipur, 1920. Ravi Shankar Shukla standing, making his declaration. Asgar Ali moved beside him. The words hanging in the air: We are no more Hindu and Muslims, but Hindustanis in the strictest sense.

slides.text: In July 1920, under the chairmanship of Ravi Shankar Shukla, a public meeting was organized at Raipur. It was resolved to support the Non-Cooperation Movement wholeheartedly. Chhattisgarh commits itself — not to an idea, but to a practice.
slides.visualDescription: The July 1920 public meeting in Raipur — a large outdoor gathering under the chairmanship of Shukla. The resolution being passed to support Non-Cooperation. Hands raised in unanimous commitment. The moment Chhattisgarh formally joins the national movement.

slides.text: Sundarlal Sharma was active in the untouchable salvation program even before the Congress took it up as a cause. He made Harijans equal participants in religious ceremonies. He was, as Gandhi would later say, a guru in this work.
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma at a temple entrance — holding it open for Harijan families to enter. Upper-caste onlookers watching, some hostile, some moved. A zamindar doing what no one expected. A man ahead of his era. Gandhi's later words true even now.

slides.text: Writers like Rai Bahadur Hiralal, Madhav Rao Sapre, Padumalal Punnalal Bakshi, Jagannath Bhanu, and Thakur Jagmohan Singh were engaged in the service of the Hindi language — building the cultural infrastructure of nationalism alongside the political.
slides.visualDescription: A literary gathering in Raipur — writers and poets reading to an audience by lamplight. The Hindi language as a weapon of unity. Each writer's face showing the conviction that culture is also politics. Ink and language as tools of freedom.

slides.text: In August 1920, the Congress adopted the Non-Cooperation Movement. For Chhattisgarh, this was not a new idea but a new name for what its people had been doing since 1825 — refusing to accept the illegitimacy of foreign rule.
slides.visualDescription: The Congress session of 1920 — the Non-Cooperation resolution being passed. Chhattisgarh delegates raising hands. The camera pulling back to show the map of Chhattisgarh — and then pulling further back to show where it sits in India. One movement, many fronts.

slides.text: In the Dhamtari region, farmers began their protest against the canal water tax even before Gandhi's arrival. Babu Chhotelal Srivastava led the Kandel Satyagraha with courage and discipline — a model for what was about to grow into a national movement.
slides.visualDescription: Babu Chhotelal Srivastava in Kandel village, 1920. Farmers assembled around him in flooded paddy fields. The canal visible behind them. The British water tax notice being read aloud and collectively refused. A small act of non-cooperation made monumental.

slides.text: The government's irrigation department accused the farmers of Kandel of stealing water from the canal. It was the month of August, raining heavily. There was enough water in the fields. The charge was false and everyone knew it.
slides.visualDescription: Kandel village in monsoon — August rain, flooded paddies, the canal itself overflowing. A British irrigation officer reading out the charge of water theft. The farmers looking at the rain, then at the officer. The absurdity of injustice made vivid.

slides.text: The policy of repression: cattle seized during farming season, Rs 4,030 confiscated from farmers. Narayan Rao Meghawale and Pt. Sundarlal Sharma joined the Satyagraha. The protest grew beyond a local dispute into a national symbol.
slides.visualDescription: British officers seizing cattle from Kandel farmers during the peak farming season. Farmers watching helplessly. Then Narayan Rao Meghawale and Sharma arriving — the local becoming national. New energy entering the movement. Solidarity across the region.

slides.text: December 1920. The Congress session was about to be held in Nagpur. Sensing the situation, Pt. Sundarlal Sharma went to Calcutta — because Gandhi was about to come from Calcutta to Nagpur. He would bring Gandhi to Chhattisgarh.
slides.visualDescription: December 1920. Pt. Sundarlal Sharma at Calcutta station — looking for Gandhi among the crowds. A mission of enormous consequence reduced to one man looking for another man in a railway station. The intimacy of the moment. Finding Gandhi.

slides.text: Sharma informed Gandhi about the Kandel Satyagraha and accompanied him to Raipur. The same pattern as Champaran — a local leader going to Calcutta to bring Gandhi. Gandhi understands: his presence alone is the pressure.
slides.visualDescription: The Champaran parallel made visual: Rajkumar Shukla leading Gandhi to Champaran 1917 on the left; Pt. Sundarlal Sharma leading Gandhi toward Raipur 1920 on the right. The same pattern. The same logic. Gandhi as the weapon of the powerless.

slides.text: When the British came to know that Gandhi was coming to support the farmers of Kandel, they immediately conceded. The British accepted the demands of Kandel Satyagrahis even before Mahatma Gandhi reached Raipur. The name alone had power.
slides.visualDescription: A British telegraph machine clicking urgently. A British officer reading the incoming message with a worried expression. The anti-farmer order being withdrawn — pen to paper, the defeat invisible to the farmers who have already won. The power of a name.

slides.text: But Gandhi is still coming. The Satyagraha may have won, but the man behind the victory has not yet seen the land he has changed. Chhattisgarh — having fought for a century without him — is about to meet the man history will place at its center.
slides.visualDescription: A train crossing the Chhattisgarh border — night, stars, the forest passing. Inside a third-class compartment, Gandhi in his dhoti, sitting simply. Pt. Sharma beside him. The land approaching. The meeting of two great forces: one man and one people.

slides.text: From 1889 to 1920 — thirty years of patient, principled, persistent awakening. Newspapers, Congress sessions, social reform, fasts, Satyagrahas. The soil of Chhattisgarh was not waiting for Gandhi. It was ready for him.
slides.visualDescription: A visual summary of 30 years — Sapre's newspaper, Sharma's Janeu movement, Shukla's Congress sessions, Kandel Satyagraha. A montage of awakening. The land fully alert, fully organised, fully committed. Ready. Waiting. Prepared.

slides.text: Madhavrao Sapre. Vamanrao Lakhe. CM Thakkar. Pt. Ramdayal Tiwari. Pt. Sundarlal Sharma. Ravi Shankar Shukla. Thakur Pyarelal Singh. E. Raghavendra Rao. Ghanshyam Singh Gupta. Babu Chhotelal Srivastava. The architects of the third era.
slides.visualDescription: A gallery of ten portraits — the architects of Chhattisgarh's modern freedom movement. Each face in its own frame, arranged like a parliament of conscience. Names beneath each portrait. These are the people who prepared the ground.

slides.text: Each one came from the soil and worked for the soil. Some were zamindars, some were lawyers, some were writers, some were farmers. The freedom movement of Chhattisgarh was not a movement of one class — it was a movement of one people.
slides.visualDescription: The spectrum of Chhattisgarh's freedom fighters — from zamindar to farmer to writer to lawyer. All in one frame, standing together. The diversity of the movement as its greatest strength. Different hands, same fist. United purpose.

slides.text: Chhattisgarh Mitra — the first newspaper — gave the movement words. The Congress committee gave it structure. The Janeu movement gave it moral credibility. The Kandel Satyagraha gave it a national connection. Now Gandhi will give it his presence.
slides.visualDescription: Four symbols of the awakening: a newspaper, a Congress flag, a sacred thread, and a canal. Then Gandhi's silhouette approaching. Each symbol contributing to the moment. The architecture of the movement complete — now comes the arrival.

slides.text: The Goraksha Song still echoes. The charkha still turns. The fasts still mean something. The names of the dead are still spoken. Chhattisgarh has been awake for thirty years. Now it is about to meet the man who will become its symbol.
slides.visualDescription: Chhattisgarh at the moment before Gandhi's arrival — a land vibrating with thirty years of accumulated energy. The charkha spinning, newspapers being read, prayers being said. A people at the peak of readiness. The train approaching.

slides.text: In small village called Kandel, the farmers have already won. The water tax has been withdrawn. The Satyagraha has succeeded without violence, without weapons, without bloodshed. A new era has already begun — before Gandhi has even arrived.
slides.visualDescription: Kandel village — the canal water flowing freely, the farmers in their fields. The British order withdrawn. A small victory on a quiet field. No fanfare. Just farmers farming. And the knowledge that they did this themselves, with truth as their tool.

slides.text: Thirty years of awakening. From Sapre's newspaper to Sharma's Janeu movement to Shukla's Congress committee to Srivastava's Satyagraha. The foundations are laid. The house of freedom is being built. Gandhi is almost here.
slides.visualDescription: A house being built — foundations of newspaper and ink, walls of Congress organisation, roof of Satyagraha. Then: a train arriving in the distance, its headlight visible through the forest. Gandhi approaching. The final piece of the architecture.

slides.text: In a small village called Kandel, the farmers are at peace. In Raipur, the platform is being prepared. In Calcutta, a man in a dhoti is boarding a third-class compartment. Next: Episode 6 — The Water and the Tax.
slides.visualDescription: Three simultaneous images: Kandel farmers at peace, Raipur station platform being decorated with flowers, Gandhi boarding a third-class compartment in Calcutta. Three worlds about to converge. Title card: Episode 6 — The Water and the Tax.
